en: The Jātaka:
The Sixth Book, the Chapter on the Unobstructed (Avāriyavagga)
7. The Sirikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka “Who is this one with a dark complexion,
yet not unpleasant to behold?”
“Who are you, or whose daughter are you?
How may we know you? “I am the daughter of the Great King.”
Because of my fierce nature toward Virūpakkha,
people know me as Kālī, the unfortunate one, the ill-fated one.
“Grant us the opportunity we request;
let us dwell in your presence.
“In what kind of virtue and in what kind of conduct [should we abide]?”
“O man, settle yourself;
being questioned by me, Kāḷī,
explain how we may come to know you.”
“Deceitful, arrogant, aggressive,
envious, stingy, and fraudulent—
such a man is pleasing to me.”
Whatever he has gained perishes for him—
he who is angry and resentful,
malicious and divisive.
Though his speech be harsh and rough,
he is dearer to me than that [other man].
"Today or tomorrow," says the man—
He does not understand his own true welfare;
when being admonished, he becomes angry and treats his superior with contempt.
A man who is addicted to sensual pleasures is ruined by all his friends;
such a man is not dear to me.
“In that I shall be free from illness.
“Go away from here, you dark one;
this does not exist among us.”
“Go to another country,
to market towns and royal capitals.
“I too know that,” he said.
This is not found among you:
there are those in the world who,
though lacking fortune, amass great wealth.
“I am a deva and my brother;
we two shall both dispel it.
“Who indeed, with divine splendor...”
Firmly established upon the earth;
who are you, whose daughter are you, and how may we come to know you?
“I am the daughter of the glorious Great King Dhatarattha; I am Śrī and Lakṣmī.”
"The wise know me as one of vast wisdom;
grant us the space we request,
that we may dwell in your presence."
“In what kind of virtue and what kind of conduct do you place your trust in a man? O Lakṣmī,
being asked by me, tell me.”
"How shall we know you?
[The Buddha replied: "Whether it be cold or even heat, wind and sun, or gadflies and serpents;"
He who, constantly engaged day and night, has overcome all hunger and thirst,
does not let pass the opportunity when its time has come.
Thus he was pleasing to me and settled there:
free from anger, a friend to all, generous,
endowed with virtue, honest, and upright.
A companion who is friendly, gentle in speech,
and humble in conduct even when he has attained greatness—
in such a person I find great delight.
Just as one might perceive the color of the ocean's waves,
so too toward friends or enemies,
the superior or the equal, or even the inferior—
Whether one is acting for one's own benefit or for the harm of others,
one should always behave with kindness both openly and in private;
one should never utter harsh speech.
I belong to both that dead man and that living one;
whoever among these two gains me, the fool,
revels in sensual pleasures as if they were lovely glory.
I avoid that one of such appearance who walks in crooked ways, like a heap of dung;
he brings misfortune upon himself.
One makes oneself unlucky;
for neither luck nor unluckiness is made by one person for another.
The Sīrikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka, the seventh.
